item.title: Binder Jetting Process Optimization: Predicting Powder Spreading Via Rheology and Enhancing Jetting Performance through Machine Learning
item.description:
Friday, August 14, 2026 at 2 PM

Location: Mechanical Engineering Building

  Speaker: Wesley Combs Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Mechanical Engineering Location: Mechanical Engineering Building 128 Binder jet 3D printing (BJ3DP) is a prominent powder-based additive manufacturing (PBAM) technique responsible for the production of high-performance parts in multiple industries including the aerospace, automotive, medical, tooling, and weapons fields. Low-density green parts are constructed by an iterative approach involving the spreading of powder into smooth layers and the subsequent deposition of binder droplets to form solid cross-sectional regions. A high-temperature densification process known as sintering is typically conducted to yield high-density end-use parts. Prior to sintering, powder flow in both the dry spreading and wet jetting systems is highly influential to green part dimensional accuracy, surface roughness, and mechanical properties. Furthermore, high-quality green parts tend to produce good end-use parts. The efficiency of BJ3DP can be increased through a variety of means, including qualification testing and analysis software. Powder flowability is often tested prior to printing to inform material selection and powder design, especially when dealing with previously unqualified materials, particle size distributions (PSDs), and powder treatment methods. Additionally, many machine learning (ML) tools have been developed for real-time powder bed inspection as well as part quality prediction. However, the majority of existing analysis in these two realms is specifically tailored to powder bed fusion, the other major PBAM technique.   A collection of BJ3DP powder flow analyses and jetting phase ML models are presented herein with various direct applications. First, an extensive study of powder rheology and additive manufacturing suitability is conducted on extraterrestrial regolith simulants. Space travel and colonization efforts are supported by mass hopper flow design according to Jenike Stress Theory and landing site suggestions informed by in situ resource utilization PBAM. Three Ti64 alloy powders commonly used in BJ3DP received additive manufacturing suitability factors (AMS) only 26-46% better than coarse lunar highland simulant (LHS-1) and only 33-51% better than Martian simulant with high sulfate concentration (MGS-1S). This increases confidence in using actual regolith as AM feedstock material and helps inform which types of lunar and Martian soil might perform best. Next, a similar experimental study is completed with a fully-recycled nickel superalloy called M247 and three conventionally-sourced steel powders (2205, 316, and 17-4). The feasibility of powder reclamation is supported by the relatively exceptional flow characteristics of M247, which outperforms the steel powders in terms of AMS by around 20%. A review of correlations between powder properties and flow parameters in metal powders shows that this was largely due to the high density and adequate particle size of M247. This demonstrates that the significant reduction in material cost provided by re-atomization does not necessitate a loss in powder spreadability. Moving on to the ML models, a set of multilayer perceptrons are trained to use PSD parameters to predict jetting-induced particle motion and saturation. High accuracy was exhibited by the model as it received low testing dataset mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE) between 5.9% and 16.7% for the four predicted macro-parameters. These values are considerably lower than the threshold value of 25%, which was based on the variation of true output data between powder beds with nearly identical PSDs. Models are designed to reduce heuristic printing and are trained on simulations executed with an in-house computational fluid dynamics and discrete element method framework. The models can be used to determine an important user-defined jetting parameter for binder jetting printers. They can also be used to identify an optimal PSD that minimizes green part porosity and dimensional error caused by particle displacement and terminal speed. The remaining ML model developed in this thesis is a physics-informed long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network that forecasts BJ3DP ejection volume, speed, and height. The LSTM model conducts direct multi-step forecasting over a 1 millisecond horizon based on printing process parameters and recent particle ejection history. The model's predictions yielded a testing dataset $R^2 > 0.9$ and low MAPE values of 24%, 14.8%, and 2.08% for average ejection volume, speed, and height. These error values were significantly less than the following MAPE values found for 63 pairs of time series with identical printing process parameters: 99% (volume), 58% (speed), and 15% (height). In the future, the model could be deployed to assist real-time monitoring by providing rapid printing process parameter modification to improve part quality. The model could also identify anomalous printing more quickly than manual human intervention, reducing unnecessary printing waste. Collectively, powder rheology and machine learning are leveraged to provide useful information and helpful analysis tools to improve BJ3DP within ISRU efforts, powder reclamation cycles, and day-to-day industrial printing. https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/95736070182?pwd=d3HLaWwkyjyJgxIPlb707zKek120rb.1 (Department : Mechanical Engineering)

item.title: Froggy Night
item.description:
Saturday, August 15, 2026 at 7 PM

$37 member / $52 nonmemberInstructor: Dr. Cassidy Johnson Ages 21+ Hop on over for a wet, wild night! Enjoy refreshments (frog-themed snacks, coffee, and Saint Arnold Brewing Company beer) while you learn all about the strange and wonderful world of frogs, from their croaking courtship to their mysterious metamorphosis. Weather permitting, we’ll also go for a hike to search for frogs and other nocturnal creatures. Please dress for the weather and wear walking shoes. register online Instructor bio: Dr. Cassidy Johnson has a B.S. and M.S. in Biology at Texas A&M University – Corpus Christi and a Ph.D. in Biochemistry & Cell Biology from Rice University. She loves teaching biology and is currently an Assistant Teaching Professor for Rice BioSciences. She fell in love with local amphibians while working for the Houston toad ex situ conservation program at the Houston Zoo. She is also passionate about the protection and restoration of Texas prairies and is on the board of the Native Prairie Association of Texas and was previously the president of the Coastal Prairie Partnership.

From Houston Arboretum & Nature Center

item.title: Parallel Algorithms for Performance Analysis at Exascale
item.description:
Monday, August 17, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: Duncan Hall

  Speaker: Jonathon Anderson Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Computer Science Location: Duncan Hall 3012 Performance analysis is critical for the development of high-performance computing (HPC) applications targeting exascale supercomputers. State-of-the-art performance tools are unprepared to handle the complex and large application binaries, unprecedented performance data volume, and widespread GPU accelerators on these platforms. Ultimately, current tools fail to provide detailed performance insights at the full scale of an exascale supercomputer, taking significant time or compute resources in postmortem processing, or sacrificing critical detail for responsiveness.   This dissertation addresses these issues by accelerating key algorithms for postmortem performance analysis, these are correlation-bound problems where the ample parallelism is limited by the need for "correlation" between inputs. Our parallelization approach produces efficient, dense parallelism for such problems by exploiting the reorderability between key operations in carefully chosen data representations. To handle large application binaries, we introduce a novel parallel control flow graph (CFG) construction algorithm with provable correctness and validated results. Our new implementation in Dyninst achieves parallel speedup as high as 25x, and accelerates a downstream performance analysis tool by up to 8x, producing detailed binary analysis for multi-gigabyte binaries in mere minutes. To handle massive performance data at scale, we introduce a new streaming aggregation (SA) algorithm for performance data aggregation that provides efficient, dense shared-memory parallelism, and a hybrid MPI/SA algorithm that incorporates conventional distributed-memory parallelism. The combination of SA and sparse data formats developed by others accelerates HPCToolkit's analysis of large-scale application performance by as much as 81x. Using it, we successfully analyzed the performance of a real-world exascale application on a single compute node, spending 0.012% of the application's compute budget. To handle complex heterogeneous code using GPU accelerators, we introduce a novel directed calling context graph (DCCG) representation for CPU, GPU, and hybrid CPU/GPU calling context that provides detailed performance analysis for heterogeneous codes without costly space expansion. Combined with a hash-based identifier methodology to improve parallelism, our new representation accelerates multi-node MPI/SA by as much as 2x. Much of the work described in this dissertation has been integrated into upstream projects and deployed on real-world exascale platforms, supporting the development of scientific HPC applications at exascale. item.title: The Technology Leadership Advantage Series
item.description:
Tuesday, August 18, 2026 at 12 PM

Location: Ion, 4201 Main Street, Houston, TX, 77002, United States

Register here: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/1995696286315?aff=oddtdtcreator Technology Isn’t Your Competitive Advantage Anymore. Leadership Is. Why High-Growth Companies Win Long Before They Write Another Line of Code Technology has never been more powerful or more accessible. Cloud infrastructure, enterprise software, AI models, development tools, and specialized technical capabilities that once separated companies are now available to almost everyone. Yet companies with access to remarkably similar technology continue to produce very different results. The difference is increasingly leadership. As companies grow, technology decisions stop being purely technical decisions. They become decisions about growth, capital, customers, product direction, risk, organizational design, and competitive position. And the leadership model that helped a company reach one stage of growth may not be the leadership model it needs for the next. Join Ram Prasad, CEO of Delence, for an executive conversation about where competitive advantage is moving and why high-growth companies need to build technology leadership before growth exposes the gap. This isn’t a technical presentation about tools, platforms, or the latest AI trend. It’s a conversation about leadership, growth, technology, and the decisions that shape enterprise value. What We’ll Discuss Why access to technology is becoming less differentiated Why leadership and judgment become more valuable as technology becomes more accessible How growth changes what companies need from technology leadership Why organizations can add engineers, platforms, and tools without improving execution Why companies sometimes outgrow the leadership model that got them here Why AI creates an executive leadership challenge, not simply a technology opportunity How strong technology leadership connects business strategy, product, technology, AI, and execution How to recognize leadership gaps before they become growth constraints Who Should Attend This session is specifically designed for CEOs, seeded startup founders, presidents, investors, private equity leaders, operating partners, and board members of growth-stage B2B technology and technology-enabled companies. It will be particularly relevant if your organization is experiencing rapid growth, increasing technology complexity, product scaling challenges, AI investment, or questions about whether the current leadership structure is ready for the next stage. If technology decisions are increasingly becoming CEO, board, investment, or growth decisions, this conversation is for you. One Question to Consider Before You Arrive Is your leadership team built for the next three years and not the last three? About Ram Prasad Ram Prasad is CEO of Delence and an executive technology leader focused on the intersection of technology, product, AI, and business growth. Throughout his corporate career, Ram has worked with executive teams navigating the decisions that emerge as organizations grow when technology becomes more complex, product priorities compete, AI creates new possibilities, and decisions that were once technical begin affecting growth, risk, and enterprise value. His perspective is built around a simple idea: Growth has a leadership problem. Ram speaks and advises on executive technology leadership, AI strategy, product strategy, scaling, and the leadership decisions that turn technology into business advantage. About Delence Delence provides executive technology leadership to growth-stage B2B technology and technology-enabled companies. Through Fractional CAIO, CTO and CPO leadership, Delence works alongside CEOs and executive teams when the business needs senior technology, product, or AI leadership, but a permanent executive hire may not yet be the right answer. Delence connects business strategy, technology, product, AI, and execution, bringing executive ownership to the decisions that become more consequential as companies grow. This isn’t staffing or recruiting. It is executive leadership for the stage the business is entering.

item.title: Concrete Cosmos: Composing Skate Architecture
item.description:
Wednesday, August 19, 2026 at 12 PM

Location: TX

In Concrete Cosmos: Composing Skate Architecture, Shane Yee presents skate architecture qua architecture, framing the skatepark as a paradigmatic yet unacknowledged achievement of the contemporary moment, characterized by adaptive reuse, the blurring of public and private space, an emphasis on lifestyle recreation, and the ascent of subcultural practices into mainstream culture. Skate spaces manifest in fluid, naturalistic configurations, converging with land art and anticipating parametric/ digital aesthetics; yet despite this sophistication, the language and principles of the discipline remain largely unarticulated. Drawing on a half-century history of skatepark design (1976-2026) and his own work at Skate Ecosystems, Yee offers a chronological series of architectural close readings, examining design intentions, ordering logics, and formal arrangements. The lecture establishes skate architecture as an emergent field with significant cultural, spatial, and spiritual implications, capable of producing elevated human experiences. About Shane Yee Shane Yee earned his Bachelor of Architecture degree from NewSchool of Architecture & Design in San Diego, California. Mr. Yee has a broad range of experiences and capabilities in all phases of project planning, design and construction- from acquisition through operations and maintenance. He has designed award-winning projects including residential, multifamily, civic, religious, master planning, and of course, skate spaces. As an officer in the United States Navy Civil Engineer Corps, Mr. Yee expertly designed & managed DOD projects with a total value of 100+ million to include Design-Build, DBB, and MILCON construction. Mr. Yee is a member of the American Institute of Architects, Society of American Military Engineers, and US Green Building Council.   This program is in conjunction with Kinetics of Urban Movement, on view at the Architecture Center Houston from June 18-September 26. Exhibition Sponsors and Community Partners Kinetics of Urban Movement is funded in part by the City of Houston through Houston Arts Alliance Cherries Wheels Honey Skate Club Houston Parks and Recreation Department Houston Skate Academy Select Skate ECOSYSTEMS Southside Skatepark

item.title: Defective Futures: Disability and Eugenics in American and British Literature (1896 – 1936)
item.description:
Wednesday, August 19, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: Herring Hall

  Speaker: Stacie Cruz Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: English Location: Herring Hall 255 "Defective Futures: Disability and Eugenics in American and British Literature (1896 – 1936)" interrogates the ways that novels in the late 19th to early 20th centuries utilize eugenic logic and discourse, arguing that the widely popularized concept of "defectiveness" allows us to think about the interconnecting logic behind the marginalization of particular bodyminds. To this end, I focus on the ways in which novels of the period apply and also (often at the same time) critique eugenic discourse. Utilizing the widespread use of the concept of defectiveness as a term that predates our current understandings of disability, I interrogate the shifting borders between who is or is not defective depending on who is wielding the term. Analyzing works by authors such as Virginia Woolf, Charlotte Perkins Gilman, and H.G. Wells, I analyze how novels represent their relationship to the future and how they narratively imagined and created futures where various populations do or do not exist, regardless of whether the narrative itself is critical of the project of eugenics as a whole.   Each chapter critiques supposed dichotomies such as perfection and deformity, humanness and animality, and madness and rationality. And it interrogates widely held beliefs, past and present, about what a body is, and what it should do, and what a mind is, and should do. This project centers rather than marginalizes the limit cases that most scholarly discussions of the future ignore: those whose bodies and minds require us to examine our discomfort about allowing pain, defectiveness, and bodymind suffering into the future. I suggest that the eugenic logic that inflects the novels I analyze likewise influences how we think about the future today. While many of us understandably desire the creation of more just futures, I nonetheless caution that understanding the future as a utopian place where things will be "better" than they currently are often relies on eugenic thinking that eliminates "defective" populations altogether. Defense Zoom Meeting: https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/94213221284?pwd=O6W0zhOPlxf4dEZiOOcoNdGdHRyKtd.1 (Meeting ID: 942 1322 1284 / Passcode: 1) One tap mobile: +13462487799,,94213221284# US (Houston) Join instructions: https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/meetings/94213221284/invitations?signature=6y2-3NwMfNUMEY1Ehp6Ha2A28K9fiFiQTIQEOtEvOu4 (Department : English)

item.title: Park Conversations: Remembering and Honoring the Soldiers of the 3rd Battalion, 24th Infantry Regiment
item.description:
Thursday, August 20, 2026 at 8 AM

Location: Clay Family Eastern Glades, 6500 Memorial Dr, Houston, TX, 77007, United States

Join us for a free audio story exhibit at Clay Family Eastern Glades Beginning August 20, Memorial Park Conservancy and the Buffalo Soldiers National Museum invite the public to Clay Family Eastern Glades for the annual return of our historic interactive audio installation, Park Conversations: Remembering and Honoring the Soldiers of the 3rd Battalion, 24th Infantry Regiment. The exhibit will be available to experience on-site through September 27. Can’t make it to the exhibit? All stories are available online. Click Here to learn more and listen now. The history of Memorial Park and Camp Logan Before Memorial Park, the land was Camp Logan – a U.S. Army training camp built in the spring of 1917, just weeks after the United States entered World War I. That summer, African American soldiers of the 3rd Battalion, 24th Infantry Regiment, one of the Army’s four “Buffalo Soldiers” regiments, arrived to guard the camp’s construction. In the aftermath of the tragedy on August 23, 1917, the battalion was disarmed and transferred. What followed was the largest court-martial in American military history, resulting in the execution of 19 soldiers and life sentences for 63 others. That verdict stood until November 13, 2023, when the U.S. Army formally set aside the convictions of all 110 soldierstried in the case. The Army also committed to correcting the soldiers’ service records, making their descendants eligible for benefits their families had been denied for a century.   Exhibit Details: Presented in partnership with the Buffalo Soldiers National Museum, the installation uses onsite audio stories to bring this history to life throughout Clay Family Eastern Glades. Where: Clay Family Eastern Glades, 552 East Memorial Loop Drive, Houston, TX 77007 When: August 20 – September 27 Cost: Free and open to the public Bring headphones. The audio is designed for personal, uninterrupted listening Parking: Paid parking available onsite at a rate of $2 for 3 hours. Free parking is available in adjacent lots.

From Memorial Park Conservancy

item.title: Mapping Houston's Innovation Ecosystem
item.description:
Friday, August 21, 2026 at 10 AM

Location: Ion – Conference Room 027, 4201 Main St, Houston, TX, 77002

Facilitated by Wade Pinder, Ion’s Mentor in Residence Houston’s startup and innovation ecosystem is as vast and dynamic as the city itself, full of opportunities, resources, and talent. Yet, navigating it can be challenging—especially for those unfamiliar with its many parts. Whether you’re an entrepreneur, investor, educator, student, community leader or curious professional, this session will offer valuable insights into how Houston’s innovation ecosystem works and how you can find your place within it. Discover the Houston Ecosystem’s Flow Facilitated by Wade Pinder, the Ion’s Mentor in Residence, this session will help participants map out the journey needed to take an idea from concept to a mature company. Wade brings years of experience in product management, community building, and mentoring entrepreneurs to the table, offering a thoughtful and informed perspective to guide this exploration. The heart of the session lies in exploring a dynamic mind map that Wade has created and continues to refine—an ever-evolving, community-driven tool that grows alongside Houston’s innovation ecosystem. Attendees will not only learn about the ecosystem’s flow but also have the opportunity to contribute to it by identifying gaps, sharing knowledge, and adding their insights. This session will center on the stages of a company’s growth journey, exploring the essential elements that drive it forward. Participants will examine the role of financial capital, from early fundraising efforts to securing the resources needed for scaling, and how these milestones align with a company’s progression. The discussion will also delve into the human element of growing a business, highlighting the evolving talent and expertise required to navigate the entrepreneurial journey. Additionally, we’ll explore the importance of “social capital”—the networks, support systems, and relationships that play a critical role in moving ideas to market and sustaining long-term growth. Ion’s Vision Helping the community better understand the local ecosystem reflects the Ion’s commitment “to being the home for Houston’s innovation community.” By fostering connections, creating opportunities, and sharing perspectives, the Ion is building a transformative culture that strengthens Houston’s economic resiliency and celebrates the entrepreneurial journey. From forming an initial entrepreneurial idea to the prototyping phase to scaling a business, this Houston Ecosystem Mapping session aligns with the Ion’s goals to support innovation, attract talent, and build a vibrant ecosystem. Who Should Attend? This session is ideal for: Entrepreneurs looking to understand greater Houston’s resources. Investors curious about the local startup landscape. Professionals and students wanting to connect with the innovation community. Anyone passionate about Houston’s growth as a hub for innovation and entrepreneurship. Innovators who have recently moved to greater Houston and are looking to get “plugged in” to the local scene. Community leaders and service providers that support (or want to support) the innovation ecosystem. Register today for this chance to explore Houston’s ecosystem, uncover its flow, and help shape its future.

item.title: The role of working memory in predictive processing during sentence comprehension
item.description:
Friday, August 21, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

  Speaker: Yu Lu Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Psychology Location: BioScience Research Collaborative 706 Language comprehension is supported not only by integrating incoming words with prior information but also by using the preceding context to predict upcoming information. Prediction is an important process that contributes to processing efficiency. However, less is known about how predictive processing relates to general cognitive resources. I addressed this issue by examining the role of verbal working memory (WM) in prediction during sentence comprehension using several methodological approaches, examining eye-movements, behavioral measures, and EEG components. Experiment 1 used the visual world paradigm to examine the relation of individual differences in semantic WM, phonological WM, visual-spatial WM, processing speed, and other verbal factors to verb-mediated anticipatory eye movements. Critically, semantic WM but none of the other individual differences measures independently predicted the anticipatory eye movement effect. Experiment 2 used a sentence-completion task to examine the role of WM in sentence-final word predictions. Sentence WM load was manipulated by including conditions with prediction-irrelevant clauses placed either before or between prediction-relevant information. Global prediction accuracy declined as information load increased and further decreased when irrelevant information was at an intervening position. Participants also became more likely to generate locally supported predictions based on adjacent context. When examining individual differences factors, semantic WM, but not phonological WM, was a significant predictor. Experiment 3 tested whether the global-to-local shift in predictions would also appear in a comprehension task without overt production demand. Participants read short and long sentence contexts followed by globally expected, locally expected, or implausible endings while EEG was recorded. Longer contexts reduced acceptance of globally expected endings and increased acceptance of locally expected endings. The N400 was graded by ending type but was not modulated by sentence length. In contrast, the late frontal positivity showed a Length x Ending interaction, suggesting that information load affected later prediction revision. Together, the findings suggested that prediction involves both a more passive and an active component, that automatic semantic activation operates alongside resource-dependent mechanisms that require maintaining and combining prior context. Semantic WM appears especially important in the active prediction process, supporting the construction and maintenance of the meaning representation from which predictions are generated. When earlier context becomes less accessible, prediction and interpretation shift toward emphasizing recent local information.   (Department : Psychology)

From Rice University - Open to the Public

item.title: Fourth Saturday Phenology Walk
item.description:
Saturday, August 22, 2026 at 9 AM

Fourth Saturday of the Month9:00 – 11:00 amFree, donations appreciatedAll ages, minors must be accompanied by an adult Meet in front of the Nature Center building Discover the hidden seasonal rhythms of nature firsthand on our guided Phenology Walks, where we track the life cycles of different plants across ecosystems, from the first spring bud burst to winter dormancy. You’ll learn how shifting weather patterns and climate change influence the timing of these important events in our local ecosystems and how you can become a community scientist, contributing vital data from your own backyard to a global research initiative. These relaxing morning walks are led by scientists from Rice University and staff from the Arboretum. We welcome nature enthusiasts of all ages, however kids 12 years and younger must be accompanied by a guardian. Learn more about the study of phenology and ways you can contribute at https://www.usanpn.org/nn Community Science Partner

item.title: Inprint Andrea Bajani & Claire Vaye Watkins Reading
item.description:
Monday, August 24, 2026 at 7:30 PM

Location: Congregation Emanu El, 1500 Sunset Boulevard, Houston, TX, 77005

General admission tickets will go on sale on Monday, August 3, 2026 at 12 pm. Season tickets are on sale here. Andrea Bajani and Claire Vaye Watkins will read from their new novels, respectively, The Anniversary (translated by Geoffrey Brock) and Yellow Pine, followed by an on-stage conversation led by professor and National Book Critics Circle Award finalist Lacy M. Johnson. The evening will conclude with a book sale and signing. The event is presented as part of the 2026/2027 Inprint Margarett Root Brown Reading Series.  Andrea Bajani is one of the most recognized and lauded authors of contemporary Italian and European literature. His many novels include If You Kept a Record of Sins, called “astonishing” by The New York Times, and Every Promise, which won the Bagutta Prize, the oldest Italian literary prize. A self-described existential writer, he often examines the personal, philosophical, and political, while confronting the unanswerable. A professor and international writer-in-residence at Rice University, Bajani joins us with his latest novel, The Anniversary, which won the 2025 Strega Prize, one of Europe’s major literary awards. Currently being translated into more than 25 languages, The Anniversary is a subtle yet heartrending portrait of an abusive marriage in patriarchal Italy and a son’s liberating decision to cut contact with his parents. The Times Literary Supplement writes, “Bajani’s prose is sharp and brims with psychological insights . . . Perhaps its most salient feature—in deft translation by Geoffrey Brock—is its skill at depicting alienation . . . Like Albert Camus, Bajani is a poet of estrangement.” Claire Vaye Watkins has been called “the most riveting voice of the unsalvageable West” (Los Angeles Times). Her debut novel Gold Fame Citrus, inspired by the Californian drought and by the lives of outcasts in the desert, blends climate fiction with environmental history. Born in Bishop, California and raised in the Mojave Desert on the Amargosa River, Watkins is also the author of the novel I Love You But I’ve Chosen Darkness and the short story collection Battleborn, winner of the Story Prize, the Dylan Thomas Prize, and the New York Public Library’s Young Lions Fiction Award. A National Book Foundation “5 Under 35” honoree and a Guggenheim Fellow, Watkins comes to Houston with her newest work Yellow Pine, described by author Megha Majumdar as “an exhilarating novel about a woman in the Mojave desert who wants to be a mother one more time, wants to love freely and arrange her life freely, wants to live outside the maze of money and ads and being sold to, a novel with huge and electric convictions.” Lacy M. Johnson is a Houston-based professor, curator, and activist, and is author of The Reckonings and The Other Side — both National Book Critics Circle Award finalists — and Trespasses. She is editor, with the designer Cheryl Beckett, of More City Than Water: A Houston Flood Atlas. She teaches creative nonfiction at Rice University, where she is the Director of the MFA in Creative Writing Program, and is also the Founding Director of the Houston Flood Museum.

From Inprint Houston

item.title: Full Day Continuing Education
item.description:
Tuesday, August 25, 2026 at 9 AM

Location: Architecture Center Houston, 902 Commerce St., Houston, TX, 77002, United States

Urbanism Continuum CE day   9:00-9:30am Breakfast and Registration 9:30-10:45am / Presentation Building Bridges: Collaborative Placemaking in the Bayou City – 1.25 AIA HSW Presented by Michael Robinson, PLA, ASLA, Principal, SWA Group Michael is a landscape architect focused on the intersection of infrastructure and public space. He leads the design and implementation of complex park, trail, and civic landscape projects, connecting regional systems into cohesive, accessible environments. His work spans planning through realization, coordinating multidisciplinary teams and public agencies to deliver resilient, buildable solutions. With a background in both architecture and landscape architecture, he brings a systems-based approach that integrates environmental performance, mobility, and user experience into high-performing public landscapes. 11:00-12:00pm / Presentation  Universal Design: Building Accessible and Healthy Spaces – 1.00 AIA HSW (Barrier Free) Presented by Kyle J. Mutz, Director, University of Houston / Justin Dart Jr. Student Accessibility Center Kyle is the Director of the Justin Dart Jr. Student Accessibility Center at the University of Houston, where he champions accessibility, inclusion, and student success. Drawing from both his professional expertise and lived experience growing up with a disability, Kyle is committed to creating equitable opportunities for all. A former U.S. wheelchair racing athlete, he brings a unique perspective on disability advocacy and is dedicated to advancing the legacy of Justin Dart Jr. through education and empowerment.   12:00-12:30pm – Break for Lunch    12:30-1:45pm / Presentation  From Paint to Policy: How Tactical Urbanism Became a Capital Project – 1.25 AIA HSW & 1.25 LA/CES HSW Presented by Ed Pettitt, MPH – President of Columbia Tap and Urban Planner with Asakura Robinson Ed is an urban planner and One Health specialist whose academic path spans human biology at Cornell University, global health and healthcare management at the University of Texas School of Public Health, and doctoral studies in Urban Planning and Environmental Policy at Texas Southern University. In addition, Ed is also the President of the Columbia Tap Trail.  He provides organizational leadership by guiding the board, strengthening partnerships, advancing strategic initiatives, and overseeing programs that support equitable community development along the Columbia Tap Trail. 2:00-3:15pm / Presentation + Tour Reclaiming Main Street: Designing a Lasting Legacy in the Public Realm  – 1.25 AIA HSW & 1.25 LA/CES HSW Presented by Alex Ramirez, PLA & Sarah Smith, PLA, CDT, Design Workshop Alex is a Principal in the Houston studio at Design Workshop, with expertise as both a landscape architect and urban designer. His diverse experience spans across the private and public sectors, involving every phase of the design process—from conceptual planning and site analysis to construction documentation and detailed observation. Alex is dedicated to delivering top-tier work by crafting innovative design solutions for plazas, streetscapes, parks, and open spaces. His approach integrates social, cultural, economic, and environmental considerations, ensuring that each project enhances the surrounding neighborhoods and communities in meaningful ways. Sarah is a landscape architect in our Houston studio with a passion for the outdoors, thoughtful design, and creating meaningful places. From concept through construction, she brings creativity, attention to detail, and a collaborative approach to projects ranging from parks and corporate campuses to urban streetscapes. Sarah earned her Bachelor of Landscape Architecture from Louisiana State University and is an active member of ULI, Central Houston, and ASLA.   Continuing Education Credits: AIA = 4.75 HSW LA/CES = 3.75 HSW   Individual classes are not available for the event. Pre-registered pricing includes breakfast and lunch. Parking is not included. A minimum of 3 business days’ notice is required to receive a full refund if you need to cancel your reservation. Online registration will close Thursday, August 20 Onsite registration is available for day of (breakfast and lunch is NOT included)

item.title: Current Research in EEPS: Dr. Bridger Ruyle, NYU Tandon School of Engineering
item.description:
Thursday, August 27, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: Keith-Wiess Geological Laboratories

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are anthropogenic compounds that contain at least one –CF3 or –CF2– group and are known as forever chemicals because they cannot fully mineralize in the environment. Although essential for modern agriculture, medicine, refrigeration, and electronics, among other industries, PFAS contamination poses risks to human health and contributes to climate change. Most research and public attention focuses on a few PFAS. This narrow focus overlooks the many hundreds/thousands of additional PFAS known as precursors that can transform into stable, terminal products in the environment. This presentation will highlight recent field work, experimental results, data synthesis, and modeling efforts aimed at improving precursor quantification using organofluorine mass balances and environmental fate, including the importance of soil retention and transformation rates. These studies will be used to discuss the role of precursors on the severity and timescales of PFAS contamination at major point sources to the environment including firefighting training facilities, wastewater treatment facilities, and farmlands.

From Rice University - Open to the Public

item.title: NASA Tech Talks
item.description:
Thursday, August 27, 2026 at 6 PM

Location: Ion, 4201 Main Street, Houston, TX, 77002, United States

We want HOU! Join us to discover NASA’s toughest tech challenges–and apply your skills and expertise to solve them.In these presentations, occurring the fourth Thursdays of the month, Mr. Montgomery Goforth and other aerospace subject matter experts will discuss the technology development challenges faced by NASA’s Johnson Space Center and the surrounding Aerospace community in our ongoing efforts as the hub of human spaceflight. Presentations will focus on the ways in which these challenges, and the associated opportunities, can be leveraged by Houston’s innovation community.Join us after the talk for drinks and networking at Second Draught!Past NASA Tech Talks have included: Montgomery B. Goforth discussing NASA Intellectual Property suitable for commercialization by small/start-up companies; Jared Daum discussing Orion’s parachutes and risk identification and mitigation that are showstoppers for the spaceflight parachute industry; Kevin Kobylka discussing current Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) capabilities and needs; and Nick Skytland, Chief Technologist at the Johnson Space Center (JSC) and Director of the Business Development and Technology Integration Office. Future NASA Tech Talks will include: dual-use (space/terrestrial) technologies in the areas of: Avionics / Communication / Sensors Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology for ultra-long lived wireless sensors Power Storage and Distribution Autonomous & Robotics Systems Extra-Vehicular Activity (EVA) Systems Virtual/Augmented Reality in Human Spaceflight Training & Execution Human Health & Performance / Human Systems Research About the Speakers Montgomery B. Goforth has more than 40 years of experience as both Engineer and Manager in a variety of highly technical space and defense-related efforts.  After working for a small defense contractor specializing in anti-submarine warfare, he joined NASA’s Johnson Space Center in 1990.  He has held leadership positions in multiple JSC Directorates and Program Offices. In his current role as Assistant Director of the JSC Engineering Directorate, he has established a framework to better focus Engineering’s efforts towards Human Spaceflight technology and systems development consistent with JSC and Agency goals for exploration. He has used this framework to guide Engineering’s internal investments and external partnerships supporting Lunar and Mars Exploration. Mr. Goforth was born in East Texas, raised in Southern California and Arizona, and graduated from Rice University (BSME 1982, MSME 1987). NASA Tech Talks topics include dual-use (space/terrestrial) technologies and focus areas in: Avionics / Communication / Sensors Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology for ultra-long-lived wireless sensors Power Storage and Distribution Autonomous & Robotics Systems Extra-Vehicular Activity (EVA) Systems Virtual/Augmented Reality in Human Spaceflight Training & Execution Human Health & Performance / Human Systems Research NASA Intellectual Property suitable for commercialization by small/start-up companies Orion’s parachutes and risk identification and mitigation strategies Leveraging Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology for ultra-long-lived wireless sensors

item.title: Author Talk with Dr. Pamela Toler, Author of The Dragon From Chicago
item.description:
Thursday, August 27, 2026 at 6:30 PM

Location: Albert and Ethel Herzstein Theater on the Mady and Ken Kades Stage

Join Holocaust Museum Houston for a night with Dr. Pamela Toler, Author of The Dragon from Chicago: The Untold Story of an American Reporter in Nazi Germany.      “Today we face an alarming upsurge in the spread of misinformation and attempts by powerful figures to discredit facts so they can seize control of our political and cultural narratives. These are threats American journalist Sigrid Schultz knew all too well. The Chicago Tribune’s Berlin bureau chief and primary foreign correspondent for Central Europe from 1925 to January 1941, Schultz witnessed Hitler’s rise to power and was one of the first reporters—male or female—to warn American readers of the growing dangers of Nazism.  She was one of the last to leave Berlin before it was too late.     In The Dragon From Chicago, historian Pamela Toler tells the story of Schultz’s years spent courageously reporting the news from Berlin, from the revolts of 1919 through the Nazi rise to power and Allied air raids over Berlin in 1941. At a time when women reporters rarely wrote front-page stories, Schultz regularly  reported the truth about Nazi Germany in the face of censorship and the threat of expulsion, internment, or death. The Nazis called Schultz “that dragon from Chicago.” One of her fellow correspondents called her “Adolph Hitler’s greatest enemy.” Schultz herself claimed to be “just a reporter.” Her story is a powerful account of one woman standing up for truth in an era marked by the spread of disinformation and propaganda spawned by hate.”     Books will be available for purchase by credit card.

From Holocaust Museum Houston

item.title: Ion Networking with Cup of Joey
item.description:
Friday, August 28, 2026 at 8:30 AM

Location: Ion – Lobby, 4201 Main St., Houston, 77002, United States

What is the purpose of Cup of Joey? It is to create a connected culture of coffee shop-open networking across our region. Every Friday morning, you’ll have the opportunity to meet new and expand your current networks, talk about tech, inspire innovation, and create community. So, what is the difference between a cup of joe and a Cup of Joe-Y? It is the WHY. It’s not what you do. It is why you do it! At the Ion, these are questions that we want to explore with the tech and innovation community. So, show up, be friendly, and make new connections. Know your why, and we will get to the future together. The future is only a cup away. Register Here: https://www.cupofjoey.org/

item.title: Rice360 Global Health Technologies Seminar Series: AI Driven Wearable Sensors for Maternal and Newborn Health in Low Resource Settings
item.description:
Tuesday, September 1, 2026 at 10 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

Join Rice360 for engaging conversations with leaders in global health and development as they share their expert insights on the intersection of medicine, technology and policy. Steve Xu, MD, MSc is a physician-engineer, entrepreneur, and board-certified dermatologist. He is the CEO and co-founder of Sibel Health as well as the Ruth K. Freinkel, MD Professor at Northwestern University. He received his undergraduate degree in bioengineering from Rice University summa cum laude, an MD from Harvard Medical School (Soros Fellow), and a Masters in Health Policy from The London School of Economics (Marshall Scholar). Dr. Xu has authored more than 120 peer-reviewed publications and listed as an inventor on 15 pending and granted patents. As both an NIH, Gates Foundation, FDA, and DoD funded investigator, he has led complex engineering, artificial intelligence, and clinical development efforts worldwide. As an MIT 35 Under 35 Technology innovator, his publications have appeared in Nature, Science, The Proceedings of the National Academy of Medicine, and the New England Journal of Medicine garnering press attention from The New York Times, CNN, The Washington Post, and The Los Angeles Times. Within 4 years of founding, Sibel Health has obtained six FDA 510(k) clearances, monitored more than 16,000 individuals, and launched in more than 20 countries worldwide with its ICU-grade wearable sensors for maternal neonatal health.

From Rice University - Open to the Public

item.title: Biomaterial models of brain tumors: Wrong but useful
item.description:
Thursday, September 3, 2026 at 8 PM

Location: Oconnor

Profile: Sanjay Kumar, M.D., Ph.D., is the E.H. and Mary E. Pardee Professor and Director of the California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences at UC Berkeley (QB3-Berkeley). His primary appointment is in the Department of Bioengineering (which he chaired from 2019-22), with joint appointments in the UC Berkeley Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, the UCSF Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Dr. Kumar earned his B.S. in Chemical Engineering at the University of Minnesota (1996) and his M.D. and Ph.D. in Molecular Biophysics from Johns Hopkins University (2003). He then completed postdoctoral training at Boston Children's Hospital and Harvard Medical School. Dr. Kumar has co-authored >120 peer-reviewed publications and mentored >30 graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. He and his group have been recognized with the Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE), The NIH Director's New Innovator Award, The Beckman Young Investigator Award, the NSF CAREER Award, and the Stem Cells Young Investigator Award. Dr. Kumar is an elected fellow of AAAS, AIMBE, and BMES, and he has served on the BMES and CMBE governing boards.

From Rice University - Open to the Public

item.title: Discover Nature Together Scavenger Hunts
item.description:
Sunday, September 6, 2026 at 2 PM

Free, donations appreciatedAll ages, minors must be accompanied by an adult Bring the whole family to the Houston Arboretum for free, themed scavenger hunts! Each month features a themed self-guided scavenger hunt where families can join us at our Nature Center before heading out to the trails to sharpen their observation skills and learn something new about nature. From spiders to fall foliage, every adventure is different! Please come prepared for the outdoors (closed toe shoes recommended, bring a water bottle, bug spray, etc).  Signs of LifeSeptember 6 We may not always see animals out and about, so how do we know they are here? They leave traces of themselves behind! From scat, to tracks, learn how to find the signs of life here at the Arboretum. Amazing ArachnidsOctober 10 Spiders are so much more than Halloween decorations. They fill the role of pest control specialist in our ecosystem. Want to learn more about these amazing arachnids? Then get into the Halloween spirit by learning more about spiders. Fall FoliageNovember 7 Although Houston is not known for its fall colors, there are still lots to learn about leaves! From deciduous to evergreen, here at the Arboretum we see leaves on the ground as well as in the trees all winter long. Join us and learn more about the difference between the two and why leaves are important in the fall. Animal HomesDecember 5 There is no central heating outdoors, so where do the animals go when they get cold? To their homes, of course! Burrows, leaves, nests, and so much more. Find out all the different types of animal homes and who lives in what.

From Houston Arboretum & Nature Center

item.title: SynthX "Unlocking the Clinical Potential of Chemical Innovation" Workshop
item.description:
Tuesday, September 8, 2026 at 5 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

By harnessing the expertise and resources of various groups within the TMC, this long-term series aims to bridge the gap between biomedical innovations and clinical applications, offering valuable insights to researchers from Rice and the TMC regarding biomedical challenges and potential solutions. Faculty, postdocs, students, and other researchers are invited to attend. Lunch is provided. — Prof. Lingyan Shi and her team are developing and applying new ultrafast laser scanning multimodal imaging and spectroscopic technologies, such as stimulated Raman scattering (SRS), DO-SRS, second harmonic generation (SHG), Fluorescence Lifetime Imaigng (FLIM), and multiphoton fluorescence (MPF) microscopy, for visualizing molecular events and metabolic dynamics in situ at subcellular resolution for studying aging and diseases. Prof. Shi and her team discovered "Golden Window" (from 1550nm to 1870nm) wavelength for deep optical tissue imaging (Shi et al., 2016), established PRM (Zhang et al., 2024) SRS and A-POD (Jang et al., 2023) super resolution multi-molecular imaging platform. Shi Lab is developing and applying bioorthogonal SRS imaging methods for dissecting complex cellular machinery in living organisms during aging processes and disease progression, offering powerful tools potentially for diagnosis, assessing therapeutic efficacy/resistance, as well as for mechanistic understanding of scientific fundamentals in neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, drug discovery, and aging processes.

item.title: Hatchlings
item.description:
Wednesday, September 9, 2026 at 10 AM

For children 0 – 18 months and their caregivers Babies in nature? Babies ARE nature! Babies who spend time outside are stronger, healthier, more confident, and better sleepers. Learn how to support your Hatchlings as they develop motor skills, test physical limits, cultivate their sense of wonder, and get messy in a safe place to try new things. Hatchlings will engage in outdoor nature play in this unique opportunity to interact, explore, and bond with their caregivers in the natural world. This program will be held outdoors and will include loose parts and messy play with natural sensory elements such as sand, mud, grass, sticks, leaves, and water. Space is limited and pre-registration is required for all Hatchlings classes. Select Wednesdays from 10:00 am – 11:00 am. Arboretum Member registration for Fall 2026 classes opens Tuesday, August 4 and Nonmember registration opens Tuesday, August 11. Become a Family Tree Member or above to access early registration and receive the Member rate. Pricing $12 member / $15 nonmember Per child/caregiver pair, per classMore than one caregiver may accompany a registered child. Minors must be accompanied by an adult. Upcoming Classes September september 9 september 16 september 23 November november 4 november 11 november 18 Additional Information Hatchlings classes are best for infants and toddlers who are creepers, crawlers, or new walkers up to 18 months old (not for older siblings), but even newborns benefit from sensory outdoor experiences Hatchlings will be held outdoors in rain or shine. Please dress yourself and your Hatchling for the weather and bring a spare change of clothes for your Hatchling. Hatchlings classes are for children 0-18 months and their caregivers only. Please do not bring older siblings to class. Accessibility This program is open to all abilities. Some areas where classes might be held are not stroller-friendly or wheelchair accessible. Please plan to carry your Hatchling to various locations and let us know if you need assistance with caregiver accessibility.

Join Us at The Lighthouse Open House 2026 for People who are Blind, Low Vision, or have a Disability! Date & Time:Friday, September 11, 20261 – 3:30 PM Location:The Lighthouse of Houston3602 West Dallas St, Houston, TX 77019 Event Description:Join us for the inaugural Lighthouse Open House 2026, a dynamic and inclusive event designed for people who are blind, have low vision, or live with a disability. This one-day event will feature hands-on experiences, valuable resources, and community connection opportunities all under one roof. Event Highlights:Employment Resume-building workshops and interview prep Meet-and-greet with inclusive employers Tips for navigating the workplace with vision loss Technology Hands-on demonstrations of assistive technology and low vision devices Tutorials on screen readers, magnifiers, and accessible apps Try-before-you-buy opportunities with top vendors Health & Community Resources Free health screenings (blood pressure, glucose, and more) Behavioral health and wellness sessions Diabetes education and vision-specific health tips Information on transportation, housing, and benefits assistance Access to local nonprofits, support organizations, and accessible recreation Whether you’re seeking tools for independence, looking to connect with community services, or exploring inclusive employment, this expo is for you. Please Note: Registration begins August 11. Check back soon!

Turn the volume up and the worries down—SINGO Bingo is back, and it’s here to play louder than ordinary bingo ever could. This monthly favorite blends the joy of music with the thrill of the game. item.title: Inprint Cool Brains! Series presents Rex Ogle
item.description:
Sunday, September 13, 2026 at 3 PM

Location: Meyerland Performing and Visual Arts Middle School, 10410 Manhattan Drive, Houston, TX, 77096, United States

Free and open to the public Free copies of one of Rex Ogle’s newest books for the first 100 families Presentation and Q&A by the author Meet the author followed by a book sale and signing Bus scholarships available for student groups – full scholarships for public schools, partial scholarships for private schools upon availability. For information, email info@inprint.org Discounted books available through Brazos Bookstore And more! The 2026/2027 Inprint Cool Brains! Series proudly presents award-winning author Rex Ogle, sharing his new books Fruitcake, a graphic novel about surviving middle school and finding the courage to be yourself, and Absent, a middle grade novel about three boys who skip school, told in verse, prose, and comics. Rex Ogle is the author of more than 100 books for kids, including comics, graphic novels, and memoirs—most notably Free Lunch (winner of the ALA/YALSA award for Excellence in Nonfiction), Abuela Don’t Forget Me (ALA/YALSA award for Excellence in Nonfiction finalist), Road Home (a Micheal Printz Honor and Stonewall Honor book), and middle grade graphic novels Four Eyes and Pizza Face. Under his pseudonym Rey Terciero, he has also reimagined classics as modern and diverse graphic novels, including Meg, Jo, Beth, & Amy, Northranger (nominated for both Harvey and GLAAD Media Awards), and Dan in Green Gables (nominated for a GLAAD Media Award). Born and raised in Texas, Rex now lives in Los Angeles where he writes every day—when he’s not reading X-Men, gaming with friends, or chasing his dog, Toby, trying to score a hug. Described as “funny, sad, goofy and poignant; a winner” (Kirkus starred review), Fruitcake is the third and final installment of Ogle’s highly popular Four Eyes graphic novel series, which tackles relatable middle school themes like bullying, puberty, building self-confidence, and navigating friendships. Eighth grade isn’t off to a great start for Rex. Everyone seems to be coupling up, and he’s starting to feel like an outsider—until he meets Charlotte. She’s fearless, smart, pretty, and, best of all, she likes him back. But as wonderful as Charlotte is, Rex can’t stop thinking about someone else: Drew, Rex’s childhood best friend. Suddenly, Rex is navigating feelings he never expected. With strong opinions swirling at home and church, Rex begins to question his own worth and what his feelings truly mean. Featuring Dave Valeza’s vibrant, colorful, and engaging illustrations, Fruitcake is a heartfelt story of laughter and fear, crushes and coming out, and the courage it takes to embrace who you are. With illustrations by LJ-Baptiste, Absent explores school absenteeism in a compelling, entertaining, and utterly distinct middle grade novel. With a dad in jail and a lack of teachers interested in helping him learn, Manny doesn’t see the point in anything besides skateboarding and writing lyrics. Calvin has so many responsibilities to his father and little brothers that when his bike is stolen, he can’t make it to school on time. And while Liam is studious and wants to become a doctor, he is tormented by bullies and hides out in an unused janitor’s closet instead of going to class. When the boys are thrown together in detention, they realize that they might still have a lot to learn—not just from their teachers, but from each other. Absent tells the boys’ stories in three distinct voices: Manny’s in verse, Calvin’s as a comic, and Liam’s as a prose journal. ***Please note that the book signing will be conducted on a first-come, first-served basis. Upon entering the theater, people wishing to have books signed will be given a number, and the book signing will take place in numerical order after the on-stage presentation.***

From Inprint Houston

Wilson Realty Co. began developing Woodland Heights in 1907 on 136 acres of land that was once part of John Austin's Mexican land grant. item.title: Inprint Claudia Rankine Reading
item.description:
Monday, September 14, 2026 at 7:30 PM

Location: Brockman Hall for Opera, Rice University, Entrance #18 off Rice Boulevard, Houston, TX, 77005

General admission tickets will go on sale on Tuesday, August 25, 2026 at 12 pm. Season tickets are on sale here. Claudia Rankine will read from her new hybrid-genre work Triage, followed by an on-stage conversation led by poet and Rice University professor Phillip B. Williams. The evening will conclude with a book sale and signing. The event is presented as part of the 2026/2027 Inprint Margarett Root Brown Reading Series.  Whether writing about intimacy or alienation, Claudia Rankine possesses a voice of unrelenting candor that “shimmers with wisdom and fury” (The Telegraph). A MacArthur Fellow, Rankine is the author of five collections of poetry, including her bestselling Citizen: An American Lyric, which explores what it means to be an American citizen in a “post-racial” society. A defining text for our time, Citizen won the National Book Critics Circle Award, the NAACP Image Award, the PEN Open Book Award, and the Los Angeles Times Book Prize. She is also the author of three plays, including Provenance of Beauty: A South Bronx Travelogue, which is performed on a bus ride through the Bronx; and is the editor of several anthologies, including The Racial Imaginary: Writers on Race in the Life of the Mind. Rankine returns to Inprint with her genre-defying new work Triage, which collides the lyric with narrative, memoir, image, and essay to offer her most personal and emotionally resonant writing yet. Triage follows the turbulent friendship between two characters, the narrator and the theorist, self-identified sisters struggling to define their wounded histories and their shared but separate lives. According to Jamaica Kincaid, “Claudia Rankine’s remarkable, outstanding odyssey—an account of our present, which is also our past, which is always our future—is beautifully rendered in a kaleidoscope of images and sensations. . . . Triage is exquisite.”

From Inprint Houston

item.title: National Voter Registration Day
item.description:
Tuesday, September 15, 2026 at 12 AM

Location: Houston Food Bank East Branch, 535 Portwall Street, Houston, TX, 77029, United States

Did you know that on Tuesday, September 15th, it’s National Voter Registration Day! At Houston Food Bank, we care about having your voice heard, and we are proud to provide the opportunity for you to register to vote on National Voter Registration Day! We are partnering with Harris County Tax Office and the National Voter Registration Day organization to serve as a site for Voter Registration at our Portwall location. You are eligible to register to vote if: You are a United States citizen; You are a resident of the county where you submit the application; You are at least 17 years and 10 months old on the date your voter registration application is submitted, and you are 18 years of age on Election Day. You are not a convicted felon (you may be eligible to vote if you have completed your sentence, probation, and parole); and You have not been declared by a court exercising probate jurisdiction to be either totally mentally incapacitated or partially mentally incapacitated without the right to vote. Seventy-six trombones. One unforgettable musical! Meredith Willson’s six-time Tony Award®-winning beloved musical comedy The Music Man marches into Houston with laughter, heart, and all the music you love. Following the fast-talking traveling salesman Harold Hill as he cons the people of River City, Iowa, into buying instruments and uniforms for a boys’ band that he vows to organize. Featuring songs such as “Seventy-Six Trombones,” “Trouble,” “’Till There Was You,” “Pick-a-Little,” and “Gary, Indiana,” The Music Man is a classic musical to be shared with every generation. item.title: Hatchlings
item.description:
Wednesday, September 16, 2026 at 10 AM

For children 0 – 18 months and their caregivers Babies in nature? Babies ARE nature! Babies who spend time outside are stronger, healthier, more confident, and better sleepers. Learn how to support your Hatchlings as they develop motor skills, test physical limits, cultivate their sense of wonder, and get messy in a safe place to try new things. Hatchlings will engage in outdoor nature play in this unique opportunity to interact, explore, and bond with their caregivers in the natural world. This program will be held outdoors and will include loose parts and messy play with natural sensory elements such as sand, mud, grass, sticks, leaves, and water. Space is limited and pre-registration is required for all Hatchlings classes. Select Wednesdays from 10:00 am – 11:00 am. Arboretum Member registration for Fall 2026 classes opens Tuesday, August 4 and Nonmember registration opens Tuesday, August 11. Become a Family Tree Member or above to access early registration and receive the Member rate. Pricing $12 member / $15 nonmember Per child/caregiver pair, per classMore than one caregiver may accompany a registered child. Minors must be accompanied by an adult. Upcoming Classes September september 9 september 16 september 23 November november 4 november 11 november 18 Additional Information Hatchlings classes are best for infants and toddlers who are creepers, crawlers, or new walkers up to 18 months old (not for older siblings), but even newborns benefit from sensory outdoor experiences Hatchlings will be held outdoors in rain or shine. Please dress yourself and your Hatchling for the weather and bring a spare change of clothes for your Hatchling. Hatchlings classes are for children 0-18 months and their caregivers only. Please do not bring older siblings to class. Accessibility This program is open to all abilities. Some areas where classes might be held are not stroller-friendly or wheelchair accessible. Please plan to carry your Hatchling to various locations and let us know if you need assistance with caregiver accessibility.

item.title: Unified Topgolf Pro-Am (Houston-Katy)
item.description:
Friday, September 18, 2026 at 10 AM

Location: Topgolf-Katy, 1030 Memorial Brook Blvd, Houston, TX 77084, Houston, 77084

The Unified Topgolf Pro-Am is one of the most exciting and meaningful community partnership events hosted by Special Olympics Texas, bringing together athletes, families, coaches, volunteers, corporate partners, and local business leaders for an unforgettable day of golf, laughter, connection, and community impact. Each bay includes a Special Olympics Texas athlete paired alongside five golfers, creating a truly unique experience where relationships, memories, and meaningful moments are built throughout the day. From friendly competition and team spirit to incredible conversations and shared experiences, the event is designed to bring people together in a fun and welcoming environment while directly supporting local athletes and programs. Proceeds from the Unified Topgolf Pro-Am help provide year-round sports training, competitions, health initiatives, leadership development, and educational opportunities for children, teenagers, and adults with intellectual disabilities throughout the greater Houston area. As the event continues growing each year, the Unified Topgolf Pro-Am has quickly become a tremendous opportunity for organizations and community members to make a real impact while being part of something incredibly energetic, uplifting, and memorable. For more information regarding sponsorship opportunities, team entries, volunteer involvement, or sponsorship opportunities, please reach out to Jared Kossover, Strategic Partnerships Manager with Special Olympics Texas Jared Kossover E: jkossover@sotx.org C: 737-867-9659

Acompáñanos en una caminata guiada por el Arboreto. Descubre la naturaleza, las plantas y la historia de nuestro hermoso centro natural junto a un guía. Nos reuniremos en el estacionamiento de la 610 Loop, cerca de la entrada al Centro Natural. Busca el letrero que indica el punto de encuentro. Las caminatas duran entre 40 y 45 minutos y recorren diferentes senderos. Venga preparado para estar en el aire libre (se recomiendan zapatos cerrados, una botella de agua, repelente de insectos, etc.). Caminata Guiada Inglés Septiembre 12Octubre 3Noviembre 7Diciembre 5 Español Septiembre 12Octubre 3Noviembre 7Diciembre 5 No se permiten grupos. Los grupos interesados ​​en reservar un tour privado durante la semana pueden comunicarse con Kelsey Low.   Guided Nature Hikes in english

item.title: The Brookwood Way Conference Sept 22-24
item.description:
Monday, September 21, 2026 at 9 AM

Location: The Brookwood Community Main Campus, 1752 FM 1489, Brookshire, TX, 77423, United States

Experience The Brookwood Way – A Conference That Changes Everything September 21–25, 2026 from 8:30am–4:00pm at The Brookwood Community, Brookshire, Texas This three-day conference provides an engaging, behind-the-scenes experience designed to fully immerse participants in our culture, methodology, and practices, which we call The Brookwood Way. Discover a proven, purpose-driven model that empowers adults with disabilities to live with dignity, purpose, and meaningful work. The Brookwood Way Conference is an immersive, behind-the-scenes experience at The Brookwood Community in Brookshire, Texas, created for leaders, families, nonprofits, ministries, and organizations seeking to build or strengthen thriving communities for adults with disabilities. Experience The Brookwood Way firsthand as you tour our campus, connect with our leadership team, and see a living model in action. You’ll leave inspired and equipped with practical ideas, proven strategies, and adaptable tools to help create communities where adults with disabilities can flourish. Who should attend? Individuals and organizations that are serving or desire to serve adults with disabilities Professionals who desire to create more opportunities for people with disabilities or other underserved populations Teachers, administrators, parents, church groups, healthcare professionals, non-profits or anyone seeking inspiration to make a difference $495 Early Bird Pricing (Conference Fee after Sept. 1—$550 per person) REGISTER TODAY What If Three Days Isn’t Enough? There are two PRE-Conference sessions and two POST-Conference sessions available! Choose a PRE-Conference Experience for Monday, Sept. 21: Satellite Immersion Opportunity – Get Inspired. See it in action! REGISTER HEREA unique pre-conference site visit to one of our Satellite Work Programs designed to provide a real-world glimpse into what a Brookwood-inspired start-up can look like. Both locations are generously donated spaces, reflecting our commitment to fiscal stewardship, and each visit includes a guided tour, time observing our Citizens at work, and lunch with a Brookwood leader who will share insights on startup strategy and building a mission-led program. OR Introduction to Handbells Workshop – Add music to your conference! REGISTER HERE Learn the basics of teaching handbells using a Brookwood-developed method, including proper technique for ringing handbells and handchimes and an introduction to reading adaptive notation. Helps you discover if this is an experience you would like to offer to those you serve. Choose a POST-Conference Experience for Friday, Sept. 25: Fundraising Essentials Course – Go Behind the Scenes with Brookwood’s Development Team! REGISTER HERELearn proven fundraising strategies from Brookwood’s Development Team, covering donor cultivation, foundation relationships, peer-to-peer fundraising, events, volunteer engagement, and donor management systems. OR Fundamentals of Citizen Life – Go Beyond the Tour and See how We Create Community REGISTER HERE An in-depth look at the divisions that make up Citizen Life at Brookwood: Residential, Work Program, Spiritual Life, Admissions, Medical, and Activities. Led by our department leaders, with time for Q&A.   Thank you for supporting the beloved adults with disABILITIES who live and work at Brookwood! Changing the way the world thinks about adults with disabilities Visit our Events Calendar for the full schedule of Brookwood’s upcoming events.

For children 18 months – 4 years Encourage your child’s curiosity about nature and spend time with them exploring outdoors! Children with an adult companion can join a naturalist for a story reading, a simple nature or sensory development activity, and a stroller-friendly hike on the beautiful Arboretum trails. Arrive dressed in close-toed shoes and comfortable play clothes. Be prepared for the weather including hat, sunscreen, jackets, raincoat, or rain boots, as needed. Enjoy an interesting new nature experience each week with themes such as ponds, bones, senses, and leaves.  Select Mondays9:30 am-10:15 am10:30 am-11:15 am pricing Free for Family Tree Members and above (please have member card on hand)$7 per child for nonmembers, pay at the door. No preregistration is necessary; however, attendance is limited to 20 children per session. Sign-up will take place in front of the Beautyberry Classroom. Doors will close 15 minutes after the class begins or once the session is full. Siblings who are not within the age range may attend but may not participate. upcoming hikes September 14, 21, 28October 5, 12, 26November 2, 9, 16December 7, 14, 21 TYKE HIKES EN ESPAÑOL! Is your child wild about nature? The Arboretum is the natural place to celebrate a birthday.

item.title: Hatchlings
item.description:
Wednesday, September 23, 2026 at 10 AM

For children 0 – 18 months and their caregivers Babies in nature? Babies ARE nature! Babies who spend time outside are stronger, healthier, more confident, and better sleepers. Learn how to support your Hatchlings as they develop motor skills, test physical limits, cultivate their sense of wonder, and get messy in a safe place to try new things. Hatchlings will engage in outdoor nature play in this unique opportunity to interact, explore, and bond with their caregivers in the natural world. This program will be held outdoors and will include loose parts and messy play with natural sensory elements such as sand, mud, grass, sticks, leaves, and water. Space is limited and pre-registration is required for all Hatchlings classes. Select Wednesdays from 10:00 am – 11:00 am. Arboretum Member registration for Fall 2026 classes opens Tuesday, August 4 and Nonmember registration opens Tuesday, August 11. Become a Family Tree Member or above to access early registration and receive the Member rate. Pricing $12 member / $15 nonmember Per child/caregiver pair, per classMore than one caregiver may accompany a registered child. Minors must be accompanied by an adult. Upcoming Classes September september 9 september 16 september 23 November november 4 november 11 november 18 Additional Information Hatchlings classes are best for infants and toddlers who are creepers, crawlers, or new walkers up to 18 months old (not for older siblings), but even newborns benefit from sensory outdoor experiences Hatchlings will be held outdoors in rain or shine. Please dress yourself and your Hatchling for the weather and bring a spare change of clothes for your Hatchling. Hatchlings classes are for children 0-18 months and their caregivers only. Please do not bring older siblings to class. Accessibility This program is open to all abilities. Some areas where classes might be held are not stroller-friendly or wheelchair accessible. Please plan to carry your Hatchling to various locations and let us know if you need assistance with caregiver accessibility.

From Houston Arboretum & Nature Center

Floyd Distinguished Professor of Engineering at UC Berkeley and President of the Robot Learning Foundation Talk Title: TBD When: Thursday, September 24, 2026 @ 4:00-6:00 PM Central Where: Auditorium, Duncan Hall, Rice University (6100 Main St., Houston, TX 77005) Parking: Paid parking will be available in Founder's Court Lot or the Entrance 3 (COB) Garage. Visit the Rice University Campus Maps webpage (https://www.rice.edu/campus-maps) for directions. Organizers: Ken Kennedy Institute (https://kenkennedy.rice.edu/)Speaker Bio Ken Goldberg is William S. Floyd Distinguished Professor of Engineering at UC Berkeley, President of the international Robot Learning Foundation, IEEE Fellow, co-founder and Editor-in-Chief emeritus of the IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering (T-ASE), and Co-Founder/Chief Scientist of Ambi Robotics. Ken leads research in robotics and automation: grasping, manipulation, and learning for applications in warehouses, homes, agriculture, and robot-assisted surgery. He is Distinguished Professor of IEOR, EECS, and Art Practice. Ken has published 12 US patents and over 450 refereed papers. He has presented over 600 invited lectures to academic and corporate audiences.

item.title: The Architectural History of Houston Street Skating
item.description:
Saturday, September 26, 2026 at 9 AM

Location: Tranquility Park, 400 Rusk, Houston, Texas, 77002

Join lifelong skateboarder and architectural historian Ted Barrow on a walking tour of the highlights of Houston’s Modernist and Late-Modernist architecture through a skateboarder’s perspective. The tour will cover key plazas and buildings which became local, state-wide, and eventually global skateboarding destinations from the late 1980’s to today. About Ted Barrow Theodore (Ted) Barrow is an art historian, writer, curator, and lecturer whose work bridges academic scholarship and contemporary currents. Born in Bolinas, California, he holds a Ph.D. in art history from the Graduate Center, CUNY, where he explored the Florida paintings of Winslow Homer and John Singer Sargent through an ecocritical lens. Barrow has taught at Barnard College, Baruch College, City College of New York, and the University of San Francisco. Outside of art and academia, he is a distinctive voice in skateboarding culture, known for This Old Ledge, a video series that investigates the cultural and architectural significance of global skate spots.”   This program is in conjunction with The Kinetics of Urban Movement, on view at the Architecture Center Houston from June 18-September 26.   Exhibition Sponsors and Community Partners Kinetics of Urban Movement is funded in part by the City of Houston through Houston Arts Alliance Cherries Wheels Honey Skate Club Houston Parks and Recreation Department Houston Skate Academy Select Skate ECOSYSTEMS Southside Skatepark

From AIA Houston

item.title: Fourth Saturday Phenology Walk
item.description:
Saturday, September 26, 2026 at 9 AM

Fourth Saturday of the Month9:00 – 11:00 amFree, donations appreciatedAll ages, minors must be accompanied by an adult Meet in front of the Nature Center building Discover the hidden seasonal rhythms of nature firsthand on our guided Phenology Walks, where we track the life cycles of different plants across ecosystems, from the first spring bud burst to winter dormancy. You’ll learn how shifting weather patterns and climate change influence the timing of these important events in our local ecosystems and how you can become a community scientist, contributing vital data from your own backyard to a global research initiative. These relaxing morning walks are led by scientists from Rice University and staff from the Arboretum. We welcome nature enthusiasts of all ages, however kids 12 years and younger must be accompanied by a guardian. Learn more about the study of phenology and ways you can contribute at https://www.usanpn.org/nn Community Science Partner
